why-cpp.title: Python on Earth, C++ in the air
body: The IRIS station terminal has been located. Your first objective is to transmit an initialization ping to the scout drone «Sigma». Radio signals between Earth and Mars take between 3 and 22 minutes one way, so the craft cannot wait for instructions from mission control — it must respond autonomously and immediately.

This is not a hypothetical challenge. NASA's Ingenuity Mars helicopter sampled its navigation sensors 500 times per second to stay stable in the thin Martian air. Its core flight-control software was implemented in C++.

Python served on the same mission on Earth — for orbital trajectory modeling, ground operations, and data analytics. C++ dominates where deterministic speed is essential: in high-fidelity game engines like Unreal Engine, browser runtime engines like Chromium, and aerospace avionics.

more.title: Origins of C++: from Bell Labs to deep space
body: In 1979 at Bell Labs, Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup began developing what was originally called «C with Classes». His goal was to merge the clean abstractions and organization of Simula with the raw computational performance and hardware-level control of C.

In 1983, the language was officially renamed C++. The name was coined by Rick Mascitti, utilizing C's post-increment operator `++`, which increases an integer by one. It signified an evolutionary step forward from C.

The foundational philosophy of C++ remains intact: «you don't pay for what you don't use». The language introduces no hidden background overhead behind the programmer's back, making it the bedrock of real-time robotics and flight systems.

sources.title: Bjarne Stroustrup — A History of C++: 1979—1991 (ACM HOPL-II)
NASA NTRS — FPP: A Modeling Language for F Prime
GitHub ReadME Project — Open Source on Mars

more.title: Determinism versus unexpected pauses
body: A compiled C++ program is transformed into native CPU machine instructions before execution. The processor does not interpret text at runtime, delivering predictable sub-millisecond response loops.

Languages relying on automated garbage collection (such as Python or Java) occasionally pause active execution to clean up unreferenced memory. In a desktop application, that micro-pause goes unnoticed. On an aerial drone spinning its twin carbon rotors at 2,700 RPM, an unexpected latency spike results in a crash.

first-program.title: Your first program, line by line
body: This is a complete, working C++ program. Each line serves an explicit engineering purpose.
`#include <iostream>` is a preprocessor directive that attaches the header file providing input and output streams. Without it, the compiler has no knowledge of `cout`.
`using namespace std;` instructs the compiler to look inside the standard library namespace by default, allowing shortened names.
`int main() { … }` represents the program's entry point. Execution of every C++ program strictly begins inside `main`, and all operational instructions reside between the curly braces.
`cout << "IRIS: online" << endl;` streams the text literal to the terminal output, and `endl` appends a newline marker. Every individual statement in C++ must terminate with a semicolon `;`.
`return 0;` signals to the operating system that the application executed and exited successfully.

predict-output.title: What will appear on the terminal?
body: Examine the three sequential output commands below. Predict the exact text that will be printed on the screen.
This is an initial prediction, not a scored test: you are not expected to know the answer in advance. Think through how the stream works, make your guess, and compare it with reality.
predict-output.explain: `cout` never injects spaces on its own. The space only exists because it was placed inside the quotes before `ONLINE`. A line break occurs only when prompted by `endl`.

run-it.title: Retype and send the first signal
run-it.task: Type the program into the editor manually rather than copying and pasting. Then click «Run».
run-it.hint: Pay close attention to every detail: curly braces `{ }`, quotation marks around strings, and the terminating semicolon `;`.

break-and-see.title: Break it and inspect the compiler
break-and-see.task: Delete the semicolon `;` at the end of line 5 after `endl` and click «Run». Inspect the error diagnostic printed in the terminal. Then put the semicolon back and verify that the build succeeds.
break-and-see.hint: Look for the message «expected ';' after expression». The caret symbol `^` points directly to where the compiler discovered the missing token.
break-and-see.solutionNote: With the semicolon restored, the program compiles cleanly and outputs the message.

how-it-runs.title: Behind the «Run» button
body: A C++ program cannot run straight from source code text. First, the compiler parses your code for syntax correctness and translates it into machine code, building an executable binary.

If the source code contains even a single syntax error, the compiler halts immediately. No executable file is generated, and nothing runs. That is why deleting the semicolon produced no partial text — the program never reached runtime.
how-it-runs.alt: Diagram: source code enters compiler, producing an executable that yields output. A syntax error halts compilation before execution.

drop-namespace.title: Code without the namespace
drop-namespace.task: This program has had the line `using namespace std;` removed. Run the code and read the diagnostic output. Fix the program without re-adding that line.
drop-namespace.hint: The compiler reports `cout` as undeclared and asks: «did you mean 'std::cout'?». Prefix both `cout` and `endl` with `std::`.
drop-namespace.solutionNote: `std::cout` and `std::endl` explicitly identify the standard namespace, eliminating ambiguity.

why-namespace.title: The `std` namespace
body: `cout` and `endl` are not language keywords like `int` or `return`. They are library utilities residing inside a dedicated scope known as the `std` namespace. Their canonical identity is `std::cout` — «`cout` inside `std`».
The directive `using namespace std;` tells the compiler: if an identifier is not found locally, look inside the `std` namespace automatically. This allows concise code.
Throughout this course, we will use `using namespace std;` to keep introductory listings clear. However, you now understand what `std::` signifies when reading production codebases.

more.title: Why large software systems avoid `using namespace`
body: Namespaces protect codebases from naming collisions. If two separate navigation libraries implement a `log()` function, prefixes resolve the ambiguity: `nav::log()` versus `telemetry::log()`.
Placing `using namespace std;` inside header files pollutes the global scope for any file that includes them. In self-contained educational files, `using namespace std;` is standard, clean, and safe.

find-bug-line.title: Which line contains the defect?
body: Sigma's diagnostic telemetry fails to compile. Locate and click directly on the line containing the syntax error.
find-bug-line.explain: Line 5 is missing a semicolon `;` after `endl`. While Clang flags this exact position, some compilers report line 6 — which is why diagnosing errors often requires checking the preceding line.

fill-gaps.title: Restore the missing tokens
body: Three critical components have been stripped from this program skeleton. Fill in the blanks and verify your solution.

status-panel.title: Build the Sigma status panel
status-panel.task: Write a complete program that outputs this exact three-line telemetry panel. Write each line using a distinct `cout` statement.
status-panel.hint: Start with the `main` skeleton and add three `cout` statements, each ending with `<< endl;`.

recap.title: Mission 1 recap
points: C++ is an ahead-of-time compiled language: source code is converted to machine code prior to execution. Syntax errors prevent the program from running entirely.
Program execution always starts at the `int main()` entry point and executes statements sequentially.
`cout` directs characters into the standard output stream without injecting automatic spaces; line breaks require `endl`.
Every complete C++ statement terminates with a semicolon `;`.
`cout` belongs to the `std::` namespace; `using namespace std;` enables writing concise shorthand.
